After a disappointing end to the 2026 season, a prominent MLB insider believes the Philadelphia Phillies will consider trading long-time star Bryce Harper this winter.
The Phillies entered this year with the fourth-highest payroll in MLB and big expectations. While they didn’t win the National League East, the hope was that their talent-rich roster could still go on a deep run in the postseason. Unfortunately, despite their best efforts, Philadelphia came up short in their three-game Wild Card series against division rivals the Atlanta Braves.
Following their season-ending loss on Thursday, The Athletic’s Ken Rosenthal claimed, “The Phillies at least need to kick around the idea of trading” the All-Star first baseman. A player the MLB insider feels doesn’t have an “oppressive” contract, with five years and $118 million left on the deal.
If the team pulled the trigger on a trade for the two-time NL MVP this winter, here are five teams he could end up landing with this winter.
Chicago Cubs
The Chicago Cubs had an equally frustrating finish to their 2026 campaign this week as well. However, they didn’t even get to three games, and the team with the sixth highest payroll in baseball was soundly beaten by the San Diego Padres in just two.
Chicago could lose both of their corner outfielders this winter, so Harper could fill either of those spots. Or the nine-time All-Star could be an option at DH. Either way, Harper would be a really nice addition to the lineup. Plus, like Alex Bregman, he is a strong veteran leader and player in the postseason.
Boston Red Sox
The Boston Red Sox are another team that saw their playoff run ended in just two games. In their case, it was rivals the New York Yankees who eliminated them. Harper could certainly be an option for Boston at DH. But the thing this team lacks the most, which he would address, is a proven veteran leader on the field and in the clubhouse. If he can handle the pressure of Philadelphia, Harper would be fine in Boston.
Toronto Blue Jays
This season was a massive disappointment for the Toronto Blue Jays. After being a couple of outs away from winning the World Series last fall, the Jays finished dead last in the AL East with a 79-83 record this year. So you can bet they will look to make a big move this offseason to get back into title contention in 2027.
If the Phillies actually make Harper available in trade talks, Toronto will be fascinated by the idea of pairing him with Vladimir Guerrero Jr. next season. If Guerrero Jr. can return to the player he always has been in 2027, and Kazuma Okamoto puts up similar power numbers, adding Harper to the batting order gives Toronto a spot in the order you can’t pitch around.
New York Yankees
The Yankees are still in the race to be champions in 2026. However, if they fall short of that yearly goal, the Yanks will surely look into adding a piece or two that can get them to end their 17-year title drought.
New York would need to find a new home for Giancarlo Stanton, but with only one guaranteed season for $15 million left on his deal, it may be possible this offseason. If they can trade the injury-prone five-time All-Star, a lineup with a healthy Aaron Judge, Harper, Ben Rice, and Cody Bellinger is one of the best in baseball.
St. Louis Cardinals
While the St. Louis Cardinals finished 77-85 this season, they seemed a bit ahead of schedule in their rebuild because of the upside in young stars JJ Wetherholt and Jordan Walker. The Cards are willing to make bold moves for proven stars if they feel they can help get the team to the next level or change the culture for the better. Harper could do both.
With St. Louis having a top-five farm system in MLB, they would certainly have the prospect assets to easily get a deal done.

item.content:encoded:
Forget the results, if you can. Losing two games in a row is a rounding error for a baseball team in every other month, but in October, it's definitive. Win and you're good. Lose and you're bad. In this telling, the Red Sox rapidly lost to the Yankees, ergo they're bad. I disagree, and this felt different to me, at least through the first six innings of both games, when things were still close enough. I felt like it was the beginning of the next great era of baseball's best rivalry.
Despite the result, I still think that.
Prior to this season — and maybe including it — I've felt that that the Red Sox/Yankees first-round playoff serieses haven't been all that consequential or compelling, because the teams are so obviously limited. I mean sure, playoff baseball widens the aperture of what's possible for good teams, but I thought neither team was likely to truly contend in 2021 or 2025, even with baseball's chaotic-by-design playoff system. This year is different. While the AL competition was so soft, like it was for last year's Patriots, both teams were plenty good enough to make the World Series, which is all you can ever ask.
The lack of Garrett Crochet and Aaron Judge left the series with a distinctly large cast of new main characters, personified by the starters, beloved Red Sox Nation blue-collar immigrant Payton Toll, despised Red Sox Nation white-collar emigrant elite Cam Schlittler and (sigh) Ben Rice. Central casting did its job for giving each fanbase its broadly-dreamt personification in a SP1, whether or not the personification has a representation in reality. we got what we wanted. The Yankees, with Rice and former MVP Cody Bellinger, got a little more, and their season continues.
But the broader question is: are we back? And not in a short-term sense? In the sense that the misery of the Yankees will return to the forefront of our minds on a daily basis? I hope so, because it's so much better that way. I think we are, after a needed cooling off period, and not just for the fans but for the owners and the league. Sometimes you need a moment alone. I live in suburban NY and they've hated the Astros since before COVID despite the multiple postseason matchups with the Sox, and I think older Red Sox and Yankees fans as a whole are happy for the interregnum on a broader horizon. Or maybe I'm just projecting, and it's certainly something I have enjoyed. I've had a break, and I'm ready to hate again.
That is, there's too much gold in these there hills to leave the rivalry comparatively dormant for so long. Not that you don't want to beat each other, every game, but the feeling of something far beyond that. This feeling, like a sourdough starter, needs time to regenerate; if it ends up taking 25-30 years, whih seems like an eternity in the moment, it's just sort of how it has gone on a longer time horizon. The last high point was 2003-2004, but before that it was Bucky Dent, in the fertile year of 1978. Before that, DiMaggio and Ted Williams in the pre- and post-war 1930s/40s era. Before that, 1918. So yeah. Every 25-30 years it happens. It doesn't have to be that way, but it just is.
On that schedule, I suspect or just wish we're due for a Retvrn to becoming the biggest story in baseball on a daily basis, and one that expands the reach of the game as effectively as Shohei Ohtani, who's done a decade's worth of heavy lifting. I am definitely wishcasting this toward existence, but I also think it's a real possibility for the next 5-to-10 years given how committed both organizations have been to similar projects in the last decade. Now they get to shut down the Dodgers by any means necessary this offseason and return to the top of the heap, even if they have to threaten the game's survival to do so. And you know what? They'll fuckin do it. If the Sox and Yankees aren't top of mind, it's gotta be a structural problem, right? Right?
True or not, both teams are so close to accomplishing a renovation that puts them back the center of baseball dialogue that we can almost taste it. If I'm right, the good news is that this year's loss, while a bummer, is still just an appetizer, and hopefully the last one. We're ready for the main courses. The divisional and LCS rounds beckon, and the identities of the post-teardown squads will further solidify. But the picture is coming in to focus: Schlittler will win the Cy Young; Tolle has won over everyone else. In this particularly illustrative case, the NY/Boston coding, as least as we'd like to conceive of it, is perfectly balanced, as all things should be. I hope this particular infinity war is ready to flare back up.

item.content:encoded:
NUEVA YORK — Los Red Sox de Boston aguantaron dos noches en el Bronx. Las discusiones que dejaron atrás siguen en marcha.
Los Yankees arrasaron en la Serie de Comodín de la Liga Americana en el Yankee Stadium, ganando 9-0 el martes y 9-2 el miércoles. Boston anotó dos carreras en 18 entradas.
Nueva York lo consiguió sin Aaron Judge. Max Fried y Cam Schlittler mantuvieron a los Red Sox a una sola carrera en 12 1/3 entradas. El jonrón de tres carreras de Cody Bellinger en una séptima entrada en la que se anotaron seis carreras acabó con cualquier duda en el segundo partido. Antes, Luis García Jr. rompió el empate a cero con un jonrón en la cuarta entrada ante Sonny Gray, y el as de Boston, Garrett Crochet, no consiguió eliminar a ninguno de los cuatro bateadores a los que se enfrentó.
La temporada de Boston había dado un giro radical. Los Red Sox despidieron al entrenador Alex Cora durante una racha que les dejó 14 partidos por debajo del 50 % a finales de junio. Respondieron con una racha de 15 victorias seguidas y un mes con un balance de 21-4 —récord de la franquicia— para alcanzar el puesto n.º 5.
Los Yankees han eliminado ahora a los Red Sox en dos postemporadas seguidas por primera vez. Nueva York lleva una ventaja de 4-3 en los siete enfrentamientos de postemporada, con victorias en 1999, 2003, 2025 y 2026.
Boston anotó cinco carreras en sus últimos cuatro partidos de playoffs contra los Yankees, todos disputados en el Bronx. El jonrón de Willson Contreras en el segundo partido puso fin a una sequía anotadora de los Red Sox en la postemporada de 26 2/3 entradas.
La mayoría de los años, la conversación pasaría directamente a la siguiente ronda. Esta vez, se fue por otros derroteros.
La temporada de Boston se había convertido en tema de conversación mucho más allá del Fenway Park. Una senadora estadounidense que luchaba por su supervivencia política había vinculado parte de su discurso a ella. Un magnate de los medios nacido en Massachusetts con millones de seguidores estaba dispuesto a defenderla.
El jueves por la mañana, ambos tuvieron que rendir cuentas ante un equipo de los Yankees que les había endosado un 18-2.
Un anuncio de campaña que apostaba por Boston
La senadora republicana Susan Collins, de Maine, aspira a un sexto mandato. Su campaña emitió un anuncio que utilizaba la rivalidad para enmarcar su contienda contra el líder de la minoría del Senado, Chuck Schumer, un demócrata de Nueva York y conocido seguidor de los Yankees.
El anuncio alterna entre imágenes del Fenway Park, un Schumer serio y Collins saludando a los votantes por todo Maine. La frase inicial parecía un informe de seguimiento sobre los Yankees.
«Los Red Sox saben cómo lidiar con los Yankees, y Susan Collins sabe cómo lidiar con Chuck Schumer, el súper fan de los Yankees», dice el narrador.
A continuación, el anuncio pasa del béisbol a la lealtad al estado natal. Presenta el equipo al que anima Schumer como prueba de cuáles son sus prioridades.
«Mientras Chuck Schumer anima a Nueva York, el equipo de Susan es Maine», dice el narrador.
Schumer es un blanco habitual de Collins porque los grupos demócratas vinculados a él han gastado mucho dinero en campaña contra ella. Una organización sin ánimo de lucro afiliada al Senate Majority PAC, vinculado a Schumer, invirtió 2 millones de dólares en anuncios contra Collins a principios de este año, según Axios.
Schumer responde a la guerra de anuncios contra los Yankees
Schumer tomó la palabra la mañana después de que se aseguraran el título. Cuando le preguntaron por la serie, se centró en la premisa del anuncio.
«No fueron los Yankees los que se quedaron en blanco las dos últimas noches», dijo Schumer.
El rival demócrata de Collins tampoco se libró de la serie. Troy Jackson, ex presidente del Senado de Maine y leñador del norte del estado, publicó su apoyo a Boston antes del primer partido.
«¡Vamos, Sox!», escribió Jackson en X.
La maniobra innecesaria de Portnoy
La segunda voz de Boston llegó tras el último out. El fundador de Barstool Sports, Dave Portnoy, natural de Massachusetts y seguidor de toda la vida de los Red Sox, vio cómo los Yankees celebraban en su vestuario y publicó su veredicto en X.
Portnoy se centró en la fiesta, no en el resultado. Las celebraciones con champán son habituales tras ganar una serie en la MLB, algo que una nota de la comunidad de X añadió más tarde a su publicación.
«Que los Yankees celebren con champán la victoria en la serie de comodines solo demuestra lo bajo que ha caído esa franquicia. Es muy vergonzoso», escribió Portnoy.
Un usuario sugirió que Portnoy publica una versión de la misma queja cada otoño.
«El tuit programado de cada año, jajaja. Seguro que programaste este el año pasado porque sabías que volvería a pasar», escribió un usuario de X.
En cifras: una primicia en la historia de octubre de esta rivalidad
Esta barrida le dio a Nueva York algo que nunca había conseguido contra Boston. Los Yankees han eliminado a los Red Sox en dos postemporadas seguidas por primera vez.
En siete enfrentamientos de postemporada, Nueva York lleva la delantera por 4-3, tras ganar en 1999, 2003, 2025 y 2026. Boston ganó en 2004, 2018 y en el partido de comodín de 2021.
En los últimos cuatro partidos de postemporada entre estos rivales, todos disputados en el Bronx, los Red Sox anotaron cinco carreras.
La temporada regular había apuntado en otra dirección. Boston encadenó una racha de 15 victorias seguidas y un mes con un balance de 21-4, récord de la franquicia, pero Nueva York se llevó la serie de la temporada por 7-6, coronada con una goleada de 16-1 en el último encuentro.
Los Rays son los siguientes, mientras la carrera por Maine sigue reñida
Los Yankees descansan dos días antes del primer partido de la Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana contra los Tampa Bay Rays, campeones de la División Este de la Liga Americana. El primer lanzamiento está previsto para las 18:30 h EDT del sábado en el Tropicana Field.
Tampa Bay tenía el mejor balance de la Liga Americana. Los Yankees acabaron con un balance de 6-7 contra los Rays durante la temporada regular. La disponibilidad de Judge sigue siendo la mayor incógnita en torno a la alineación y la plantilla del entrenador Aaron Boone.
Una encuesta de CNN/SSRS realizada a 880 votantes registrados, entre el 31 de agosto y el 6 de septiembre, mostró que Jackson iba por delante de Collins con un 48 % frente a un 45 %. El «Cook Political Report» califica la contienda como reñida.
Los dos candidatos sí que comparten una cosa: los dos son seguidores de los Red Sox.
La temporada de Boston ya ha terminado. La racha de los Yankees continúa este sábado en San Petersburgo, Florida. Los votantes de Maine acudirán a las urnas el 3 de noviembre.
¿Qué opinas? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

On Wednesday night, the New York Yankees beat the Boston Red Sox by a score of 9-2.
With the victory, they swept the Red Sox in the Wild Card Series.
Bob Nightengale of USA Today wrote: “The New York Yankees sweep the Boston Red Sox out of the Bronx in humiliating fashion. They outscored the Red Sox 18-2 in the wild-card series. They are off to Tampa Bay for a best-of-five AL Division Series beginning Saturday”
Judge Makes Bellinger Statement After Sweep
Cody Bellinger finished the win with two hits, including one home run and four RBIs.
After the game, Aaron Judge was asked about Bellinger when he spoke to YES Network.
Meredith Marakovits: “Last night it was Ben Rice. Tonight it was Cody Bellinger with some big hits. Those two bats in the lineup. Just how valuable are they?”
Judge: “It’s amazing. We saw Ben Rice make a lot of strides last year. I knew coming into this year he’s going to have a great year for us. And then that’s why we signed back Cody Bellinger, man. He’s built for this. He’s built for New York. He’s built for the big moment. And he continues to show up for us when we need him.”
Looking At Bellinger
Bellinger is in the middle of his second season with the Yankees.
He has also spent time with the Los Angeles Dodgers and Chicago Cubs over 10 seasons at the MLB level.
As Judge alluded to, Bellinger signed a big deal with the Yankees over the offseason.
Looking At The Yankees
The Yankees finished the regular season as the second-place team in the American League East with a 93-68 record in 161 games.
They are looking to win their first World Series title since the 2009 season.

item.content:encoded:
MLB playoff predictions 2026: Expert picks for every ALDS, NLDS series originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
October has officially arrived, just in time for the MLB postseason to ramp up.
With all four Wild Card series now over — three of which ended in two-game sweeps — just eight teams remain alive in the pursuit of a World Series title, with the Guardians, Rays, Dodgers and Brewers entering the picture after watching the first round from home.
Some of baseball's biggest stars, from Shohei Ohtani and Jacob Misiorowski to Junior Caminero and Cam Schlittler, will be on full display for the division series. On both sides of the bracket, the question will be whether the teams carrying their Wild Card momentum can now take down a well-rested heavyweight.
With a chance to reset between rounds, the best-of-five ALDS and NLDS matchups begin Saturday. Who will advance to the championship series?
With Wild Card matchups in the rearview mirror, The Sporting News predicts the 2026 MLB division series matchups.
MORE: Complete MLB playoff schedule for 2026 postseason
No. 6 Chicago White Sox vs. No. 2 Cleveland Guardians
You can certainly debate whether the Guardians (85 regular-season wins) or White Sox (84 regular-season wins) really belong on the postseason stage this season, with neither AL Central squad owning a ton of big-name star power. Regardless, the fact is that Cleveland and Chicago both find themselves with an opportunity to make a serious postseason run in a weaker AL bracket — and the White Sox have already taken advantage.
Chicago enters the ALDS the momentum of its first postseason series win since the 2005 World Series, proving in the Wild Card round that it has the power and pitching depth to challenge opponents. Cleveland, though, has better top-end starting pitching in Parker Messick, Gavin Williams and Tanner Bibee.
These two teams are well familiar with each other; the White Sox won the season series, 7-6. Cleveland's offense isn't very threatening, ranking last among all postseason teams in team OPS (.696) — this matchup will likely come down to how early the White Sox's bats can get to Guardians starters.
Saturday will mark the first time in MLB history that the Chicago White Sox and Cleveland have met in the postseason.
The White Sox began playing baseball in 1894 as the Sioux City Cornhuskers.
The Guardians began playing baseball in 1896 as the Columbus Buckeyes/Senators.
The fact that this is a divisional matchup means it will likely be close, but Chicago's momentum is hard to ignore, and there was only a one-win discrepancy between the sides in the regular season. The White Sox are finally building something serious, seemingly with a new hero every night. The power in Will Venable's lineup is dangerous enough to reach the ALCS.
Prediction: White Sox in 4
No. 4 New York Yankees vs. No. 1 Tampa Bay Rays
It's been clear since the start of the postseason that whichever AL East team emerged from the lower half of the bracket would be favored to reach the World Series. This is the heavyweight matchup of the two ALDS series, featuring elite starting pitching on both sides and some of MLB's premiere sluggers.
Of course, the massive question lingering over this matchup is how much, if at all, Aaron Judge will play for the Yankees. Even as the lower seed, if he's near 100 percent, it's hard not to view New York as the favorite to reach the ALCS; a healthy Judge, alongside Cody Bellinger, Luis Garcia Jr. and Ben Rice, takes Aaron Boone's lineup to a new level, capable of matching the all-around offensive excellence of Tampa Bay's quartet: Caminero, Yandy Siaz, Jonathan Aranda and Chandler Simpson.
The Rays won this season series 7-6, but it may be the most evenly matched division series. Both sides can roll out a trio talented starters — New York with Cam Schlittler, Max Fried and Gerrit Cole, and Tampa Bay with Drew Rasmussen, Nick Martinez and Shane McClanahan — to pair with deep offenses.
Yankees can line up their pitching as follows against the Rays:
Game 1: Gerrit Cole
Game 2: Cam Schlittler
Game 3: Max Fried
Game 4: Gerrit Cole
Game 5: Cam Schlittler
For two reasons, the Yankees are the pick here. For one, between Schlittler and arguably the best bullpen in baseball, New York is loaded with leverage arms. And the Yankees are also riding high off a dominant Wild Card series, biding time for Judge and Giancarlo Stanton to heal. Assuming those two sluggers can at least be used in some key at-bats, the Yankees' lineup is capable of changing games in an instant.
Prediction: Yankees in 5
No. 3 Atlanta Braves vs. No. 2 Los Angeles Dodgers
The Dodgers' path to becoming the first National League team to win three-straight World Series will begin with a matchup against a 94-win Braves squad fresh off a Wild Card win over the Phillies.
Los Angeles' rest advantage could be significant. Even if he's not pitching, Ohtani has been dealing with lingering injury concerns over the last few months. A week off between his last regular season game should only benefit him, not to mention the Dodgers' ability to line up their loaded starting rotation however they choose. With the Braves using Chris Sale in two games against Philadelphia, he may not be available early in the NLDS.
The Dodgers and Braves have built quite the postseason history. 👀🔥
2013 NLDS — LAD def. ATL
2018 NLDS — LAD def. ATL
2020 NLCS — LAD def. ATL
2021 NLCS — ATL def. LAD
2026 NLDS — ??? 🤔 pic.twitter.com/mHhbDO9gDX
The top of Atlanta's lineup is potent enough to make this an interesting series, and the team did beat the Dodgers five times in the regular season, but Ronald Acuna Jr., Austin Riley and Ozzie Albies will have to meet the moment in the NLDS. Yoshinobu Yamamoto has pitched well against Atlanta in his career, as have Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow.
Even if the Braves' bats can keep things close, it's hard to imagine Atlanta's pitching staff beyond Sale being able to contain Ohtani, Freddie Freeman, Kyle Tucker and Mookie Betts over a five-game series. The Braves are a good team, but the Dodgers are far too talented to fall this early in the bracket.
Prediction: Dodgers in 4
No. 4 San Diego Padres vs. No. 1 Milwaukee Brewers
This matchup pins baseball's best team all season, Milwaukee, against one of its hottest over the past month, San Diego. While the Brewers are the clear favorites here, between the best starting pitcher in the game this season and a deep lineup that plays to contact, the Padres do pose some interesting challenges, going 4-2 against Milwaukee in the regular season.
On one hand, San Diego has stars made for October. As shown in the Wild Card round, when the top of the Padres' lineup is on, they're a hard team to beat — Fernando Tatis Jr., Manny Machado, Xander Boegarts, Ty France and Jackson Merrill can look like one of the best 1-through-5 groups in baseball at times. Add in an elite starter (Michael King) and a strong bullpen led by Mason Miller, and there's a path for the Padres to pull off a stunner here.
Most data has shown that the more of a threat a team is to hit the ball out of the yard, the better they'll fare in the postseason. If this is finally going to be the year the Brewers reach a World Series — putting an end to their cycle of regular season success with playoff shortcomings — they'll need to slug more. This is an offense that's outstanding at making contact and getting on base, but has also continually come up short in October and finished second-to-last in team home runs (154) in the 2026 regular season.
Chances are, Milwaukee won't only be able to rely on its strong pitching staff to reach the World Series. The Brewers' bats will need some extra-base hits. But with the Padres' lackluster starting pitching depth, this is still a series the Brewers can claim even if they're not pristine.
San Diego may have some top-end talent and momentum, but the Padres can't match Milwaukee's all-around depth.
Prediction: Brewers in 4

item.content:encoded:
The night started with Cody Bellinger’s glove.
In a sentimental moment before Game 2 of the Wild Card Series, Bellinger caught the ceremonial first pitch from his father, Clay Bellinger, who played for the Yankees from 1999-2001.
But by the end of Wednesday night, it was the younger Bellinger’s bat that commanded the attention.
Bellinger went 2-for-5 with a home run and four RBI in a 9-2 victory over the Boston Red Sox in the Bronx, completing a lopsided two-game sweep as the Yankees advanced to the ALDS.
“I’m able to appreciate it in the moment,” Bellinger said afterward, reflecting on sharing the night with his father. “That was a cool moment, just a great game. Happy I was able to contribute, and we’ve got a lot more work to do.”
Continued contributions from Bellinger would go a long way in the Yankees making a deep postseason run, with the AL East-winning Tampa Bay Rays up next in the ALDS.
Bellinger takes on added importance with Aaron Judge sidelined indefinitely due to a calf strain.
He was one of the driving forces in the Yankees’ two-day demolition of the archrival Red Sox, whom they outscored 18-2. The All-Star went 3-for-8 in the series and delivered a pair of key hits in Wednesday’s clincher.
With Yankees leading by a run in the fifth inning, Red Sox manager Chad Tracy controversially removed right-handed starter Sonny Gray after 70 pitches with runners at the corners and two outs.
Tracy turned to the left-handed Erik Miller to face the lefty-swinging Bellinger, who delivered an RBI single that put the Yankees up, 2-0.
Then in the sixth, after an intentional walk to Ben Rice in front of him, Bellinger capped a six-run rally with a three-run home run against right-handed reliever Garrett Whitlock — a 360-foot drive into the right-field stands that served as the dagger.
“He’s built for this,” Judge said Wednesday during a champagne-soaked celebration in the Yankees clubhouse. “He’s built for New York. He’s built for the big moment, and he continues to show up for us when we need him.”
Bellinger, who won the 2019 National League MVP and the 2020 World Series with the Los Angeles Dodgers, is in his second season with the Yankees, having re-signed last winter on a five-year, $162.5 million contract.
Despite missing a month with a hamstring strain, Bellinger batted .264 with 17 home runs, 73 RBI and a .768 OPS in 132 games. He was worth 4.6 WAR (wins above replacement), in part because of his excellent defensive work in left field, too.
“This offseason, there were a couple of other teams involved,” Clay Bellinger said in August of his son’s free agency. “But I said, ‘If you can sign back with these guys, and you go out there and you win a world championship to add to this legacy, there’s no better place in the world to play baseball.’”
The elder Bellinger would know, as the former utility player won World Series with the Yankees in 1999 and 2000.
Now, the Yankees’ World Series aspirations rest in large part with Bellinger, who continues to carve out his own pinstriped legacy.
Despite hitting left-handed, Bellinger is actually better against left-handed pitching than he is against righties, making his bat even more crucial for balance in a Judge-less lineup that’s loaded with lefties.
The Yankees went 15-for-35 (.429) against left-handers in the Red Sox series, with Bellinger recording two hits in those matchups and another top-of-the-order lefty batter in Rice totaling three.
“No secret sauce,” Bellinger said of his reverse splits. “For me, just take it as another at-bat. Felt like when I was playing baseball coming up, didn’t hear too much about the match-ups. I was just playing baseball.”
After hitting .214 in his first postseason with the Yankees, Bellinger is off to a .333 start to this one. Wednesday’s home run was Bellinger’s 11th in the postseason and his second in nine playoff games with the Yankees.
“I feel like I was able to enjoy that one,” Bellinger said. “Just a home game in Yankee Stadium, it’s a really fun atmosphere. It’s fun to play. And hopefully we get many, many more this month.”

La segunda jornada de la Serie de Comodín en la temporada de las Grandes Ligas (MLB, por sus siglas en inglés) selló el adiós de los dos cubanos más mediáticos de la Liga Americana: el slugger Yordan Álvarez y el lanzador Aroldis Chapman.
Los Astros de Houston, de los que Yordan fue bujía a lo largo de la campaña, cayeron en apenas dos juegos ante los Medias Blancas de Chicago, mientras a los Medias Rojas de Chapman los frenaron en seco uno de los exequipos del cerrador holguinero: los Yankees en Nueva York.
Los Medias Blancas ganaron este miércoles 7-3 en Houston y completaron la barrida sobre los Astros. Así, dejaron sin opciones al tunero de seguir ensanchando la mejor campaña de su trayectoria, coronada con el liderazgo de bateo del circuito con promedio de .316, además de despachar 42 jonrones y luchar por la Triple Corona hasta el final del calendario regular.
Houston, we don’t have a problem pic.twitter.com/NmPM6SCndJ
— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) October 1, 2026
Poco pudo aportar Yordan a la causa, al irse en blanco en cuatro visitas al plato. Con ello dejó su producción ofensiva en la postemporada en solo un imparable en los ocho turnos oficiales sumados por él en los dos choques disputados.
La suerte estuvo siempre del lado visitante, pues Chicago anotó cuatro veces en el primer episodio ante el abridor Hunter Brown, ayudado por errores defensivos. En lo adelante, los Astros solo pudieron responder con jonrones solitarios de José Altuve, Jeremy Peña y Cam Smith.
Este duelo era el de mayores expectativas entre los aficionados cubanos dada la presencia en el bando de Chicago del joven antesalista Miguel Vargas, quien tuvo su mejor temporada en la fase preliminar, pero no ha tenido un feliz estreno en la instancia decisiva.
El habanero volvió a fallar en cinco turnos, lo que, unido a un similar desempeño en el choque anterior, lo mantiene a la espera de su primer imparable en la postemporada.
Esta vez el protagonismo recayó en Chase Meidroth, autor de un vuelacercas de tres carreras, y en el bullpen encabezado por Erick Fedde y Jordan Hicks, quienes no permitieron hits en cuatro entradas combinadas para apuntalar la victoria de Anthony Kay.
3-RUN POSTSEASON HOMER FOR CHASE MEIDROTH! pic.twitter.com/39yNEWjiLt
— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) September 30, 2026
Boston desarmado
En el Yankee Stadium, los dueños de casa complacieron a sus parciales con la segunda victoria seguida ante los Medias Rojas de Boston, esta por 9-2. El éxito dejó sin opciones de supervivencia a sus archienemigos históricos y marcó el cierre de temporada para su cerrador estrella Aroldis Chapman.
Max Fried trabajó seis entradas, con seis ponches y una carrera limpia, y fue respaldado por Cody Bellinger al conectar jonrón y producir cuatro anotaciones.
CODY BELLINGER THREE-RUN HOMER
IT’S 8-1 YANKEES! pic.twitter.com/gUQC8CJQb9
— MLB (@MLB) October 1, 2026
Luis García Jr. también firmó un significativo aporte al batear de 5-3 con otro vuelacercas, signo de la oportunidad de los bateadores del Bronx, quienes ligaron de 9-6 con corredores en posición de anotar.
Sonny Gray cargó con la derrota, que tampoco pudieron evitar varios relevistas, entre ellos Garrett Crochet y Garrett Whitlock.
Chapman, sin oportunidad de cerrar un juego ajustado en la serie de comodín, tuvo una entrada de actuación en la que ponchó a los tres bateadores que enfrentó.
Con ese despliegue se convirtió en el primer jugador nacido en Cuba con participación en 10 postemporadas de MLB, y en el segundo de Latinoamérica con 10 o más experiencias de este tipo, solo superado por el legendario panameño Mariano Rivera (16).
¡EL MISIL SIGUE HACIENDO HISTORIA! 🇨🇺
Aroldis Chapman se convierte en el 2do jugador nacido en Latinoamérica en participar en 10 diferentes #Postseason uniéndose a Mariano Rivera. pic.twitter.com/1VjtJcLAZO
— MLB Español (@mlbespanol) October 1, 2026
Además, con los tres ponches recetados llegó a 76 ponches en octubre, para colocarse en el listado histórico de relevistas por detrás de Rivera (110) y Kenley Jansen (94).
Con 38 años, el holguinero cerró una de sus mejores experiencias de las últimas temporadas. A lo largo del tramo regular fijó una efectividad de 1.92 carreras limpias por juego, con 35 salvamentos y 71 ponches en 51.2 entradas.
Sin Cachorros en juego
Las cosas también fueron bien en casa para los Padres de San Diego, al despachar por segunda ocasión sucesiva a los Cachorros de Chicago, esta vez con pizarra de 4-1.
Gavin Sheets conectó jonrón de dos carreras, al tiempo que Xander Bogaerts y Ty France aportaban dos hits cada uno.
Summer’s over, we’re on to October. pic.twitter.com/I4KRWqSyyf
— San Diego Padres (@Padres) October 1, 2026
La ocasión fue propicia para que el relevista cubano Adrián Morejón debutara en la serie lanzando dos entradas en blanco, con un hit permitido, sirviendo de puente hacia los cerrojos de Mason Miller y Jason Adam.
Todo lo contrario sucedió en Atlanta, donde los Filis de Filadelfia lograron equilibrar el pulso con una victoria 4-3 sellada en 10 entradas, que extendió hasta este jueves la definición del trámite.
Kyle Schwarber, Bryce Harper y Alec Bohm combinaron su poder con jonrones para la causa de los visitantes, mientras que el joven Andrew Painter retiraba a los bateadores de Atlanta durante tres entradas en blanco para quedarse con la victoria.
Well, that was wild pic.twitter.com/FpU4KdGxXo
— Philadelphia Phillies (@Phillies) September 30, 2026
El relevista cubano Raisel Iglesias trabajó un inning por los Bravos, con un hit permitido y sin tolerar carreras.
A la espera de esta decisión, los Medias Blancas se alistan para enfrentar a los Guardianes de Cleveland en la Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana, que arranca el venidero sábado 3 de octubre.
Por su parte, los Yankees enfrentarán con el mismo objetivo a los Rays de Tampa Bay, que cuentan en su filas con los cubanos con el cubano Yandy Díaz y Victor Mesa Jr.
En la Liga Nacional, San Diego pactó su choque con los Cerveceros de Milwaukee —el mejor equipo de la temporada regular con 103 victorias— y los actuales campeones, los Dodgers de Los Ángeles, con el cubano Andy Pagés entre sus referentes, aguardan para conocer su primer rival en la ruta hacia la conquista de su tercera Serie Mundial consecutiva.

NEW YORK – This is only the first checkpoint of a postseason journey the Yankees hope will stretch deep into October. But if they had to choose an opponent to send home first, few would be more satisfying than the Red Sox.
For the second consecutive year, that’s exactly what they did. Their celebration reflected that, with corks popped and bubbly spraying in every direction.
Luis García Jr. hit an early homer and Cody Bellinger delivered a three-run dagger late as the Yankees trounced the Red Sox, 9-2, on Wednesday night at Yankee Stadium, sweeping the two-game American League Wild Card Series.
“Being able to celebrate with your teammates after a playoff series win, it doesn’t get old,” said left-hander Max Fried. “This is what we start practicing in February for. This is where we want to be. So it’s just about playing our game, having fun, and hopefully we’ve got a couple more of these we can do.”
The victory vaults the Yankees into the AL Division Series against the Rays, with Game 1 scheduled for Saturday at Tropicana Field. The Yankees plan to start either Gerrit Cole or Carlos Rodón, pitching coach Matt Blake said.
Following Schlittler’s lead, Fried permitted three hits over six innings of one-run ball, then leaned on the bats to do the rest against the Yankees’ most historic rival. This had been expected to be a low-scoring series, but New York made it lopsided.
“As I said all year, but even going into this series, that was a scary team to us – especially as well as they pitch,” manager Aaron Boone said. “I’m just really pleased with how we played. We’re going to enjoy that, and excited to get our shot at a really good Tampa [Bay] club.”
Imported to supply power with captain Aaron Judge on the injured list, García provided a big fourth-inning swing that represented an overwhelmingly left-handed lineup’s first dent against one-time Yankee Sonny Gray, who was touched for a pair of runs before exiting to a loud chorus of boos in the fifth.
Born in New York and counting himself as a Yankees fan before moving to the Dominican Republic in early childhood, García beamed as he crossed home plate, pointing into the crowd. He hit 30 home runs during the regular season, seven after being acquired from the Nationals in August.
“I only have one word – unbelievable,” García said. “You feel the crowd, you feel the fans. You feel everything right now. This experience for me, it’s unbelievable.”
Bellinger caught the ceremonial first pitch from his father, Clay, then delivered a run-scoring single to greet left-hander Erik Miller in the fifth – the second time in as many nights Miller surrendered a run to the first batter he faced, having allowed Ben Rice’s first of two homers in Game 1.
The Yankees broke it open with a six-run sixth, sending 10 batters to the plate. Rookie shortstop George Lombard Jr. collected his first postseason RBI, setting up Austin Wells and Ryan McMahon to knock in runs.
“This shows what we can do,” Lombard said. “We’re obviously a great clubhouse, a great group of guys. When everything’s going our way, when we’ve got all our guys competing like we are now, I think we can do a lot of great things.”
Bellinger capped the rally, slugging a Garrett Whitlock changeup into the seats. This time, Boston intentionally walked Rice to face Bellinger. It didn’t work.
“I was very surprised they were willing to face Cody Bellinger, a guy who absolutely thrives with runners in scoring position and has done it his whole career,” Rice said. “Interesting decision.”
Said Bellinger: “That was a cool moment. I feel like I was able to enjoy that one. Home game in Yankee Stadium, it’s a really fun atmosphere. It’s fun to play, and hopefully we get many, many more this month.”
Willson Contreras and Nick Sogard homered for the Red Sox, who went 26 innings without scoring a postseason run before Contreras’ sixth-inning shot off Fried – a streak that dated back to Game 2 of last year’s AL Wild Card Series in the Bronx.
Given that drought, the Yanks’ firepower was too much to overcome.
“You’re thinking we're going to play closer games,” Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said. “They swung the bats extremely well. You've got to give them credit. It was frustrating.”
Now the Yankees turn their attention to the Rays, who claimed the division by 4 1/2 games during the regular season and won seven of 13 meetings with New York this year.
But October can change everything, and right now, the Yankees are confident they will.
“I know we didn’t win the division,” said Judge, who is hoping to be activated for the next round. “We weren’t the No. 1 seed, got put in the Wild Card. But we’re not trying to make a statement. We’re trying to play our game and take care of business.”

In the words of a Yankee legend, it was dèja vu all over again in the Bronx last night as Cam Schlittler continued crafting a legend of his own. Just like last season, Schlittler delivered a gem of a performance against the Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, staking New York to a 1-0 series lead and giving them an opportunity to close the affair out early tonight. But unlike last year's three-game set, in which the Yankee offense never fully erupted, the lineup finally achieved escape velocity. Ben Rice and his four hits, two homers, and six RBI, led the charge — but the bottom of the lineup contributed their fair share as well.
In other words, the Yankees played the perfect ballgame last night. Max Fried will be tasked with carrying the momentum into Game 2. Fried's second season in pinstripes has been marred by a couple of IL stints limiting him to just 20 starts and 112.2 innings, but when he's been healthy, he's been just as good as in 2025. He'll be pitching on seven days' rest in Game 2 — his last appearance was an up-and-down start against the Rays, in which Tampa clinched the AL East.
As far as the recent track record against Boston, Fried has been quite effective. He only faced them twice this season: one was a short start from when he was returning from his latest injury, the other an eight-inning masterpiece in April from before the Red Sox got it together under new manager Chad Tracy. In Game 1 of last year's WCS, he provided 6.1 scoreless innings, scattering four hits three walks while striking out six. The Yankees couldn't hold onto the narrow 1-0 lead he had defended, and sabotaged their own comeback effort after loading the bases with nobody out in the ninth inning. None of that was Max's fault, of course. Provided the lineup supports him, an effort like last year's will be more than enough.
Old friend Sonny Gray never caught on with the Yankees in 2017 and 2018, but he'll have no choice but to step up under the Yankee Stadium lights with Boston's season on the line. Over his first season with the Red Sox, the steady veteran turned in yet another outstanding season, leading the AL with 18 wins (don't think that doesn't mean anything to him) and pitching to a 2.72 ERA. That's the thing about the Red Sox' pitching: they have lots of exciting youngsters like Payton Tolle, who pitched last night, but they also routinely get the most out of their veteran pitchers too. Gray faced New York twice in June and pitched well both times. The latter outing was his best start of the season by game score — one hit, one walk, nine strikeouts over 7.1 scoreless innings.
Unsurprisingly, Aaron Boone's lineup for Game 2 is nearly unrecognizable when compared with the Game 1 starting nine. It's a history-making card: according to James Smyth of the YES Network, it's the first time a team has put eight lefty batters — switch hitters not included — in the same lineup in the postseason. The portside octet includes Trent Grisham, who entered late last night for his first action off the IL. Rice will ascend to the leadoff spot, with Cody Bellinger and Luis Garcia Jr. to follow. Spencer Jones hits cleanup and plays right field ahead of George Lombard Jr., the lone righty to get the start. Jazz Chisholm Jr. draws in at the keystone, Grisham bats in the seven-spot after him, Austin Wells will bat eighth, and Ryan McMahon starts at third and will hit ninth. Naturally, expect plenty of right-handed bats to come off the bench against a lefty-heavy Boston staff once Gray's start concludes.

The Yankees made MLB playoff history in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series, starting eight true left-handed hitters to face right-handed Boston Red Sox starter Sonny Gray.
Never before had a team started that many lefty batters — not including switch-hitters — in a postseason game, per the Elias Sports Bureau.
“I saw our lineup and I assumed that was probably the case,” one of those lefties, Cody Bellinger, told the Daily News with a grin. “I didn’t know. We’ve got a lot of talent in this locker room.”
It was in stark contrast to Tuesday night’s Game 1, when the Yankees started only four left-handed batters against Red Sox lefty Payton Tolle in an eventual 9-0 win in the Bronx.
On Wednesday night, lefty-swinging first baseman Luis García Jr., second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr., center fielder Trent Grisham and third baseman Ryan McMahon all returned to the starting lineup as the Yankees sought platoon advantages.
Lefty-hitting Spencer Jones, who started Game 1 in center field, moved to right field for Game 2.
Meanwhile, righty-swinging Paul Goldschmidt, Heliot Ramos, Amed Rosario and Anthony Volpe all began Wednesday’s game on the bench after starting Game 1.
Rookie shortstop George Lombard Jr. was the only right-handed batter in Wednesday’s lineup.
Gray is actually a bit tougher against lefty batters than righties, but because the Red Sox carry five left-handed relievers, Boone said he liked having a bench full of right-handed batters that he could deploy in the later innings.
The best-of-three Wild Card Series allows for this kind of maneuvering because, given its short nature, teams are able to carry more hitters and be more aggressive with their bench moves.
The Yankees carried 16 position players in the Wild Card Series, compared to just 10 pitchers.
That likely won’t be the case in future rounds, when they would need to use a fourth starting pitcher and cover more innings with their bullpen.
But Games 1 and 2 against the Red Sox showed how the Yankees plan to approach the postseason, with matchups dictating their lineup decisions perhaps more than they have in the past.
“With this group, I feel like it’s going to take everyone,” manager Aaron Boone said Wednesday. “So that’s my plan — day in and day out, it’s going to be a little different, potentially. And that phrase ‘all hands on deck’ certainly applies to us with our team right now.”
The Yankees need to prioritize lineup creativity even more because the matchup-proof Aaron Judge is sidelined indefinitely with a calf strain.
Giancarlo Stanton — who also typically starts against righties and lefties — is currently relegated to pinch-hitting duty after missing more than five months due to three separate calf strains.
And Wednesday marked the first game started by Grisham since Sept. 4, when he suffered a hamstring strain. After being activated for the Wild Card round, Grisham entered Game 1 in the seventh inning as a defensive replacement and went 0-for-1 at the plate.
“I know he’s ready to go,” Boone said. “I liked his at-bat [in Game 1] when he came in, hit a ball well to center. I don’t know what I’m going to get from any of the guys tonight. But I’ve got a lot of confidence in who he is and what he can bring to the table.”
The Yankees became even more platoon-oriented after they acquired García and Ramos, both of whom perform to traditional splits, before the Aug. 3 trade deadline.
All of those factors led to Wednesday’s historic, lefty-loaded lineup.
“It’s super beneficial for us, because all the guys in the lineup are super tight — righties and lefties — and there will be a lot of different conversations between different guys in what they saw, how they picked it up,” Jones told The News.
“And then we’ve got a bunch of guys ready to go off the bench.”
SCHMIDT SHUT DOWN
Clarke Schmidt’s season is officially over.
The right-hander has been shut down after landing on the IL with right biceps neuritis shortly after making his long-awaited return from Tommy John surgery.
Boone said last week that it was his understanding Schmidt would be shut down, but he hadn’t confirmed it until Wednesday.
But Boone said Schmidt is doing “fine.” That’s in line with what Boone shared last week, when he said Schmidt was expected to have a normal winter to build up for spring training.
More than a year after undergoing elbow surgery, Schmidt made his season debut on Sept. 16 and recorded two outs in a relief appearance.
A starter by trade, Schmidt had hoped to help out of the Yankees’ bullpen this postseason.
But Schmidt experienced a cramping sensation as he warmed up for a second relief appearance, then returned to the IL last Thursday.
VOLPE NEWS
Volpe has a new agent, confirming to The News that he is now being represented by Scott Boras and the Boras Corporation.
Boras is baseball’s most prolific agent, representing stars such as Juan Soto, Gerrit Cole and Bellinger.
Volpe, 25, is eligible for free agency after the 2028 season.

Apple vs. Microsoft. Coke vs. Pepsi. Marvel vs. DC. Ford vs. General Motors.
All child’s play compared to Yankees vs. Red Sox.
Though seeded as Wild Cards, New York and Boston are heavyweight entries in the 2026 postseason field. And only one can advance out of the best-of-three Wild Card Series that begins -- and takes place entirely -- in the Bronx on Tuesday.
The Yankees have survived most of the season without captain Aaron Judge, while the Red Sox survived a brutal start that had them 14 games under .500 in late June.
But who will survive this short and scintillating series at Yankee Stadium? Let’s break it down, position by position, and we are sure to find the unmistakably correct prediction, right? Right?!
Catcher
Austin Wells just hasn’t produced with the consistency he did in his Rookie of the Year finalist season in 2024 or the power he had in last year’s 20-homer, 20-double campaign. He’s a fantastic framer and blocker, and that could matter more in the postseason than his bat given the pitching staff’s increased importance in a short series. But Rutschman has those same strengths, along with an elite caught stealing track record, to go with higher offensive upside in a season in which he’s posted an above-average OPS+.
Edge: Red Sox
First base
The Red Sox have a major asset, but also a major question mark in Willson Contreras. He was a monumental offseason pickup in a trade with the Cardinals. The veteran produced his best offensive season yet, with an OPS over .900 and career-highs in homers and RBIs.
But when Contreras was plunked in the hand by a pitch late in the regular season, it complicated the equation. As of this writing, it was still not clear if he would suit up for the Wild Card Series. Even if he does, he might need some time to get back in the swing of things, given the impact hand discomfort can have on a power stroke.
So the Yankees’ successful midseason acquisition of Luis García Jr. looms large here. After an offensive breakthrough with the Nationals, he’s remained an above-average producer in pinstripes, finishing off his 30-homer season. And the Yanks have a dangerous platoon option in Paul Goldschmidt, the consummate pro who still does big damage to lefties – no small tool in their chest given the lefty leaning complexion of the Red Sox’s starting staff.
Edge: Yankees
Second base
Between the trade of the disappointing Marcelo Mayer and a late-season injury to Anthony Siegler, the Red Sox are left piecing things together here with Nick Sogard and veteran Isiah Kiner-Falefa, and Sogard’s contact skills can play up in the postseason even if he doesn’t produce much power.
But the Yankees have higher upside here. Though Jazz Chisholm Jr.’s walk year saw statistical regression, he ultimately provided league-average offense with north of 40 steals. He could augment his open-market asking price with a strong showing.
Edge: Yankees
Shortstop
Trevor Story was sidelined for the Sox for about three months with a sports hernia that required surgery. He showed signs of offensive life in September, but this will nevertheless go down as one of his worst seasons at the plate in limited time.
The Yankees look like they have a star in the making in George Lombard Jr. While no one knows how the fresh-faced 21-year-old, who only debuted on Aug. 4, will perform under the bright lights of the postseason, he’s already had some huge hits for the Yanks and his plate discipline, high baseball IQ, fluid actions and plus speed all make him dangerous in a short series.
Edge: Yankees
Third base
The hot corner has been cold to the Yankees this year. Veteran Ryan McMahon’s first full season in the Bronx has been a drastic disappointment and his right-handed-hitting complement Amed Rosario hasn’t been much better. The Yankees were toying with the idea of working former shortstop Anthony Volpe here.
As for Boston, while replacing free-agent departure Alex Bregman was a tall order, a trade for Caleb Durbin, a reigning NL Rookie of the Year finalist with the Brewers, has paid enormous dividends. Durbin looked lost in the headlights for his first couple months in a major market, but his midseason ignition matched that of the club at large. He has great range at third, is among the more difficult batters in MLB to strike out and logged 25 doubles for the second straight season.
Edge: Red Sox
Left field
After getting spurned by Juan Soto in free agency the previous winter, the Yankees did not let Cody Bellinger get away. In his second season with the Yanks, the former NL MVP became an All-Star Game MVP in the midst of providing his usual disciplined, contact-and-power profile at the plate and elite defense in the grass. He’s been on this postseason stage plenty of times before.
There was hope in Boston that Roman Anthony would break out into superstardom this season. But a significant finger ligament injury early in the season got in the way, opening the door for Jarren Duran to see the bulk of time in left while producing an OPS+ more than 20% below league average. Anthony returned in late August, and it should shock no one if this postseason turns into his coming-out party. But for now, we’ve got to go with the more accomplished veteran here.
Edge: Yankees
Center field
The Sox had another late-season health scare with Ceddanne Rafaela, their rangy, speedy power-armed gem in center field. Rafaela was finishing up his finest offensive season to date when he suffered a right quad strain a few weeks back. But a clean MRI in the season’s final week allowed him to return.
Meanwhile, Trent Grisham’s September hamstring strain gave the Yankees their own center-field concern. Grisham’s absence allowed 25-year-old rookie Spencer Jones to showcase his excellent raw power and athleticism. Grisham could be back for this series. But Rafaela’s offensive breakthrough and Gold Glove defense carry the way here.
Edge: Red Sox
Right field
Judge’s calf injury is probably the biggest X-factor in the entire postseason field. The Yankees were cagey about its severity, and manager Aaron Boone said the club was preparing for a Wild Card Series without the captain. Judge was intent on trying to make his way back. But ultimately, Judge was left off the Bombers' Wild Card roster, so they'll be down one of the best hitters on the planet.
For the Red Sox, Wilyer Abreu is ready for his close-up. He was a durable doubles machine who also reached career highs in homers and RBIs, he dramatically improved his production against left-handed pitching, and he has range and a mammoth arm in right. His surge was essential in the Sox returning to the postseason.
Edge: Red Sox
Designated hitter
With Masataka Yoshida out with a hamstring strain, Boston will utilize a DH platoon that includes Roman Anthony against righties and Jahmai Jones against lefties.
In a season that has included so little Judge, the Yankees have gotten a ton out of Ben Rice. Last season’s surprise ascendence for the New England native has proven to be only an appetizer. Rice showed he can mash both lefties and righties alike in clearing the 40-homer threshold, getting selected as a first-time All-Star and earning down-ballot MVP support.
Edge: Yankees
Starting pitching
Cam Schlittler’s likely Cy Young-winning breakthrough in 2026 came on the heels of him carving up the Red Sox club he grew up rooting for in last year’s Wild Card Series. He pairs with Max Fried and Gerrit Cole to give the Yankees a terrifying top end of the rotation in this short series, even if the finish on Cole’s pitches is not yet what it was prior to Tommy John.
While the Yankees deserve the edge here, that’s not to suggest the Sox are slouches in the starting department. That they got to this point essentially without Garrett Crochet took a lot of fortitude, and Payton Tolle’s fantastic rookie campaign was one of the most fun storylines of the season. Sonny Gray remains an absolute command artist in his age-36 season, and Ranger Suarez was a terrific offseason signing who drastically limits the kind of hard contact that can change games in October.
Still, it’s the Yanks here.
Edge: Yankees
Bullpen
These are two top-five relief units in terms of both ERA and expected ERA. Both are excellent at suppressing long balls, which is crucial in October.
The Yankees have a strong ninth-inning anchor in David Bednar, whose elite ability to generate chase with his four-steam/split/curve mix can neutralize even the biggest bats. Paul Blackburn has gone from oft-injured starter to absolute force of nature in the setup role, and Brent Headrick has also undergone a massive transformation as a member of the Yankees ‘pen, for whom he has emerged as a whiff machine. The strength of the starting staff has trickled down to a Yankees bullpen that ranks among the lowest innings workloads of any relief unit in MLB this season.
With Tyron Guerrero’s recent return from injury and the presence of Garrett Whitlock, Greg Weissert and lefty Jovani Morán, the Sox are well-situated in their bridge to the ninth. And in the ninth, they’ve got the ageless Aroldis Chapman, whose age-38 season has seen him produce yet another sub-2.00 ERA, another ERA+ more than 100% better than league average and upper-echelon velo and strikeout rates. He recently returned from a late-season lat issue. Between Chapman’s presence and the possibility that Crochet’s elite arsenal impacts the ‘pen in his potential return from injury, the Red Sox earn the edge.
Edge: Red Sox
Prediction
The Yankees were the better team in record and run differential, and they did it mostly without Judge. They hold the home-field and rotation advantages, have a higher run-scoring baseline and are, therefore, the clear favorites.
All reasons why I’m taking the Red Sox in three. Because baseball.

item.content:encoded:
The MLB playoffs are here as 12 teams survived the regular season and are ready for an all-out battle for October supremacy. Each of the remaining squads has spent the last six months proving it belonged in the postseason. None of the last teams standing got here unscathed and all have glaring weaknesses that could end their seasons early.
With postseason baseball upon us, here is the fatal flaw that could derail each MLB playoff team.
Brewers: Lack of Power
The Brewers were baseball’s best team all season but that doesn’t mean they’re perfect. Milwaukee has a great rotation fronted by baseball’s new ace Jacob Misiorowski, and a good bullpen, but the lineup relies heavily on getting hits up and down the lineup. The Brewers play the 2026 version of small ball, and don’t have a ton of power. That can kill teams in October, when runs come at a premium.
Milwaukee finished the season tied for 28th in home runs (154) and 25th in isolated power (.144). The Brewers were tied for 10th in slugging (.403) and were third in wRC+ (107), but the lack of top-line power could be their downfall. Against elite pitching in the postseason, it’s much more difficult to string together hits and build big innings. Being able to get runs on balls that leave the yard is huge. Each of the last six World Series champions ranked inside the top five in regular season home runs.
Maybe Milwaukee bucks that trend, but if they don’t win the World Series, a lack of power may be the reason.
Dodgers: Health
The Dodgers have won two straight titles and at full strength, they’d be the overwhelming favorite to take home a third in a row. But L.A. has dealt with major injuries all season and the team looks more vulnerable than it has in a long time as we enter the postseason.
Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow combined to make only 22 starts this season. Both are back now, but neither has been particularly reliable—Snell left his penultimate start on Sept. 16 with a groin injury before returning to pitch four innings on Saturday. Tarik Skubal had elbow surgery earlier this year with the Tigers and hasn’t been quite as dominant as usual when it comes to limiting baserunners. Shohei Ohtani has been sidelined by knee and biceps injuries, and won’t be pitching in October. Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts and Teoscar Hernandez are showing signs of decline and have played a ton of baseball over the last three years.
L.A. is still loaded, but a few injuries to a roster that’s had its fair share of medical issues could make things dicey.
Rays: Trouble Against Lefties
It’s hard to find too many flaws here. The Rays are an incredibly balanced squad that was the best in the AL pretty much all season. One of the only red flags here is the team’s performance against lefties, and they’re likely to run into a few in the playoffs.
Against lefties as a team, Tampa Bay ranked 27th in slugging (.364), 26th in wRC+ (90) and 25th in OPS (.679). Luckily for the Rays, their best offensive players hammered lefties. Junior Caminero slashed .287/.426/.490 with eight home runs and a 152 wRC+. Unfortunately, the 23-year-old and Yandy Diaz are the team’s only players who appeared in 100-plus games and topped .700 in OPS against lefties.
That’s a weakness opponents will try to exploit in October. The Rays don’t have many holes, but good left-handed pitching could be the kryptonite that slows one of baseball’s most complete teams.
Braves: A Hole at Shortstop
The Braves have plenty of star power in the lineup and Chris Sale at the top of their rotation but they have a huge flaw at the heart of their team. Atlanta’s shortstops were among the worst offensively during the 2026 season. Ha-seong Kim is is the starter, but he had a .359 OPS with zero home runs in 147 plate appearances this season so I’m not sure that is the answer. The other option is Mauricio Dubón, who had a .719 OPS in 153 games, but that won’t work against southpaws since it means lefty Mike Yastrzemski must play left field.
Collectively, Braves shortstops slashed .241/.295/.349 during the regular season and ranked 27th with a wRC+ of 78. They also ranked 23rd in fWAR (1.6) and bWAR (-0.4). They simply haven’t gotten enough out of the position and need to find some offensive production there.
Atlanta went wire-to-wire to win the NL East and did so while not getting much from a premium position. Against elite pitching in the postseason, they’ll need production out of everyone in the lineup at some point. Carrying an empty spot will likely prove to be more damaging than it already has been.
Yankees: An Aaron Judge-Sized Hole in the Lineup
The Yankees may have baseball’s best postseason rotation and found enough offense to hold onto the AL’s top wild-card spot. But to win a World Series, they need their best player healthy and hammering baseballs. They may not have it.
Aaron Judge is trying to return for the wild-card series from a strained calf muscle, but it would be unwise to rush him back into action. Yes, New York needs his bat in the lineup, but it also needs to ensure he is available for the entire postseason, not just the first series. Ben Rice (149), Cody Bellinger (115) and Paul Goldschmidt (111) are the only Yankees with more than 300 plate appearances and a wRC+ over 100. That’s a scary lack of production from the lineup.
They need Judge’s bat back at full health as soon as possible simply because the team relies on him so much to produce.
Padres: Who Starts After Michael King?
The Padres have baseball’s best bullpen and an offense that has been clicking on all cylinders in the second half. What they don’t have is a deep rotation after injuries have decimated it.
Michael King is the team’s ace and should be reliable in that spot, but after him things get dicey. Nick Pivetta missed most of the season due to a flexor strain in his pitching elbow that cost him nearly five months. He’s back and has thrown well, but he’s only made eight starts this year. After that, it’ll be some combination of Robbie Ray and Walker Buehler. Both have been up and down this season and neither feels like a rock-solid option.
If San Diego can get decent starts and shorten games by getting the bullpen in early, things could be fine. But if the team’s starters struggle it could mean an early exit.
Cubs: A Battered Starting Rotation
The Cubs have one of baseball’s best offenses and its best all-around player in Pete Crow-Armstrong, but their pitching staff remains a patchwork mess. The team’s starting rotation has endured season-ending injuries to Cade Horton and Ben Brown, Justin Steele still hasn’t returned after elbow surgery in 2025, Matthew Boyd missed time thanks to knee surgery and a shoulder issue, and Kevin Gausman is now dealing with a shoulder injury.
Chicago will open the postseason with Boyd on the mound and should follow with Clay Holmes in Game 2, then Shota Imanaga and, if he’s healthy enough, Gausman. How bad has it been for the Cubs? Among starters, only Imanaga generated 2.0 bWAR this year. That’s a dangerous weakness to carry into the postseason when pitching becomes even more important.
Could the Cubs manage to overcome a rotation that has been battered all season? It’s possible, but that would take a herculean effort from the team’s top-ranked offense.
Phillies: Trea Turner’s Disappearing Production
Trea Turner was a key piece of the Phillies’ success in 2025, as he slashed .302/.354/.450 with 15 home runs, 36 stolen bases and a 123 wRC+ in 141 games. The team is probably wondering where that guy went.
In 157 games this year, Turner slashed .242/.297/.378 with 19 home runs, 21 stolen bases and a wRC+ of 83. His strikeout rate jumped from 16.7% to 21.0%, his xBA dropped from .270 to .242 and his xwOBA of .293 ranked in the 14th percentile. That would be manageable if Turner provided value defensively, but his outs above average dropped from 17 in 2025 to -8 this season. That’s a precipitous, ominous drop for a shortstop who’s in his age-33 season, has always depended on his athleticism and still has seven more years on his contract. Philadelphia has underachieved as a whole in 2026, and Turner is the poster child.
While he was a disappointment in the regular season, Turner has a ton of playoff experience and won a title with the Nationals in 2019. Maybe he’ll turn it around when the lights are the brightest. But his postseason track record doesn’t offer much optimism. He has a career playoff OPS of .681.
Red Sox: A Top-Heavy Offense
Boston’s comeback story this season was remarkable after Alex Cora was fired following a 10–17 start. While they were one of MLB’s best teams over the final two-thirds of the season, the offense never really clicked one through nine. As a team, the Red Sox finished 17th in wRC+ (99) and 19th in OPS (.717). And it seemed all season a few guys would come through, while the rest of the lineup struggled.
Among the team’s hitters who played at least 100 games, only Willson Contreras (151), Wilyer Abreu (112) and Ceddanne Rafaela (109) topped 100 in wRC+ to grade out as above-average hitters. The drop-off from Contreras to the rest of the roster is pretty alarming in itself, though Mickey Gasper (130), Masataka Yoshida (108) and Roman Anthony (106) all performed well in fewer than 300 plate appearances. Key pieces like Caleb Durbin (100) and especially Jarren Duran (69) had off years, while catcher Adley Rutschman slashed .222/.278/.410 with a wRC+ of 88 after arriving at the trade deadline.
Boston will have to overcome those issues throughout the lineup, particularly against the kind of pitching ahead in the postseason. The lack of offensive balance could be the team’s downfall.
Guardians: A Lineup Short of Firepower
The Guardians are in an enviable position, as they barely made the playoffs but wound up with the AL’s No. 2 seed. While they are set up for success thanks to the bracket and have an excellent pitching staff, their lineup has been anemic.
Cleveland finished the regular season ranked 27th in home runs (162) and slugging (.380), 26th in OPS (.696), 24th in runs scored (678) and 21st in wRC+ (97). Meanwhile, star third baseman José Ramírez wrapped up the worst full season of his career, slashing .235/.320/.368 with 12 home runs and a wRC+ of 92. The question is simple: Where do the runs come from? Rookie Chase DeLauter was the team’s most productive hitter after slashing .287/.363/.456 with 16 home runs and a 131 wRC+, but he doesn't have much help. Steven Kwan was second on the team in wRC+ (114), but only slugged .349, while Travis Bazzana (110) and Angel Martinez (108) were both only modestly above average by wRC+. The rest of the lineup struggled to generate offense.
After a tough battle down the stretch, the Guardians wound up with a favorable path in the postseason. But getting to the World Series will likely require unearthing some unsung heroes on offense.
White Sox: October Inexperience
The White Sox surprised everyone with their run to a postseason berth after three consecutive 100-loss seasons. The roster has been properly overhauled, with only 19.8% of the team’s plate appearances coming from players on the 121-loss team in 2024. The problem is, most of the team’s new players have little to no postseason experience.
Braden Montgomery, Munetaka Murakami and Sam Antonacci are rookies, while Colson Montgomery, Kyle Teel, Chase Meidroth and Grant Taylor are second-year players. Sean Burke debuted in 2024, but has never pitched in the postseason, and All-Star Miguel Vargas has likewise never appeared in the postseason despite coming up with the Dodgers. Maybe there’s something to be said for youthful exuberance, but there’s also the possibility that fatigue becomes a factor for players who haven’t been through a playoff chase before. Colson Montgomery posted a wRC+ of 54 after August 1, while Murakami slashed .156/.299/.375 in that stretch.
Chicago is built for success long-term, but its lack of postseason experience could be a significant obstacle in October.
Astros: A Thin Starting Rotation
The Astros finished 81–81 to win the weak AL West and notch a playoff spot. Given their record, it’s not surprising they have a ton of issues across the roster. The most glaring is their starting rotation, which is in rough shape.
Beyond Hunter Brown, Houston simply doesn’t have the kind of high-end starting pitching that wins in October. And even Brown enters the playoffs with some uncertainty, having thrown only 107 ⅓ innings this season after missing a chunk of the campaign with a shoulder injury. Peter Lambert has become the team’s No. 2 starter, but he went 8–10 with a 3.82 ERA and doesn’t possess premium stuff. Hayden Wesneski finished the season strong, but made only 11 starts all year, while Cristian Javier and Mike Burrows are both on the IL.
The rotation is so thin that the Astros are poised to open Game 1 of the wild-card series with a bullpen game to give Brown, Lambert and Wesneski rest. It’s hardly an ideal situation and there aren’t many options available for manager Joe Espada.
